statement: Ana, Bo and Cy each always lie or always tell the truth. Ana: "Exactly one of us lies." Bo: "Exactly two of us lie." Cy: "All three of us lie." How many lie?

choices.misconception: I believed all three of them without checking whether their sentences can all be true together.
I believed Ana, without noticing that Bo and Cy would then both be liars, which makes two.
I believed Cy, but if Cy told the truth, Cy would not be a liar.
I thought there was not enough information to tell.

hints: Can Cy be telling the truth?
The three sentences give different numbers, so at most one of them can be true. Test each child as the only truth-teller and check whether the number of liars then matches what that child said.
Cy cannot be truthful, because then Cy would be a liar. If Ana is the only truthful one, there are two liars, not one.

solutions.reliable: The sentences give different numbers, so at most one is true. Cy cannot be telling the truth, since a truthful Cy would be one of three liars. If all three lied, there would be 3 liars and Cy would be right, which is impossible. If Ana alone told the truth, there would be 2 liars, not 1. If Bo alone tells the truth, there are 2 liars, Ana and Cy, which matches Bo. So there are 2 liars. The transferable idea: assume one speaker is truthful and check whether the whole picture agrees with itself.

whyOnTest: Truth-teller puzzles reward testing each possibility for consistency rather than trusting any one sentence.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
